utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am in receipt of a memorandum from your legal associate, Mr. Rakic, explaining that Mr. Delic will not be testifying today. The explanation in the circumstances is accepted, but you should nonetheless make arrangements for Mr. Delic to be here to continue his testimony at the earliest time. Please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Saban Fazliu. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A change has been made. The next witness will be Muharem Ibraj, and after him, Saban Fazliu. I had a different order noted here, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to greet you all. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ibraj. Could you please introduce yourself and say something briefly about yourself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I hereby greet you. I am ready to speak the truth for things that I know. You can begin with your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us where you were born, where you went to school, where you worked, and where you lived.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of September, 1953, in the village of Osek Hilja, Gjakove municipality. I completed primary school in Skivljane village and secondary school in economics in Mitrovica e Titos. From 1972 until 1980, I had my private business, a restaurant. In 1981, I worked as a forest ranger in Erenik. In May 1998, I worked for the security of the village, and I performed this work until 14th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your village, Osek Hilja that you mentioned a minute ago, is very close to Djakovica and it belongs to Djakovica municipality, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It is attached to Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, is your village purely Albanian in terms of its population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: My village consists of 186 households, and out of these only one was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ibraj - you lived in your village all the time - were there any problems between Serbs and Albanians in your own setting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: In the past, there were many Serbs in our village. From 1980, they began to move from the village, but during the whole time they were in our village, we were always in good terms, Serbians and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, when did the problems actually start or, rather, conflicts or tensions on ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Problems began in 1998 when the terrorists, the KLA, were formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did these problems manifest themselves?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: They manifested these problems with their revolt against the Serbs, against the state, against the Albanians who were not working for them, with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that when the organisation of local security started in your area, specifically in your village or, rather, specifically in your municipality of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The local defence in Gjakove municipality began in May 1998. Every village in Gjakove municipality had two persons designated for local security. Those two persons who were able to defend their own village, those villages remained undamaged to this date. However, there were cases when they were not able to defend their villages; they were either kidnapped or killed. There were killings, arson, everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, who did you protect your villages from? The local security, who did it protect villages from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I had a comrade, an associate of mine. We made an agreement with the army and the police and the villagers in the village for the villagers not to be disturbed either by the police or the army but also by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in all villages in the municipality of Djakovica local security had been set up and that every village had two members of the local security respectively. Did you personally hold a particular position in this local security?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, we had. We worked through the municipality. I'm not quite sure, but I think that Gjakove municipality consists of 76 villages, and every village had local security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you speak about this in a bit more detail, because this is the first time that we have authentic testimony about this, authentic evidence. How were these local security members selected? Who appointed them? What was their role? I'm going to put several questions to you so that I do not burden you with a great many questions altogether.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The local security was established by the president of the municipality. Now I'm speaking only for the Gjakove municipality. The local security was established by the president of the municipality, Momcilo Stanojevic. He called from each village one person to attend meetings, and he organised meetings on village level within two days and elected persons who were able to guarantee for that certain village. For example, for Osek village, I was elected by the village. I and Mihil Abazi were able to guarantee that nobody will touch the village of Osek. And this is how it was to the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other villages? Was that the type of selection that took place? Did the villagers themselves choose their local security?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: In each village, villagers themselves elected two persons for local security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that members of the local security had uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: We had our uniforms, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The uniforms differed from the uniforms of the police. We carried the insignia on the chest and on the cap, and on the insignia it was written in both Albanian and Serbian "Local Defence." We had special permissions. We had rifles, we have truncheons, and for each village there was one vehicle assigned. There were six radios for the entire local police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ibraj. Please tell me about the collection of weapons. Could you tell me what kind of drive this was, specifically in your village, what you organised yourself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: First I would like to apologise. I had many problems, and I wasn't able to remember all the dates. I don't know the exact date, but it was sometime in the beginning, in May 1998. I and Mihil Abazi, together with two elderly persons from the village, we went to each and every house in the village and informed them to surrender their weapons. We guaranteed to them that nobody will touch them, because the president of the municipality guaranteed to us, and this is how things proceeded to the end. And within 24 hours every weapon that was taken from the KLA was brought to me. They surrendered these weapons to me. Together with two other persons from the village, I collected these weapons with two tractors and brought the weapons to SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you said just now that you collected weapons that the villagers had received from the KLA. However, it is a well-known fact that Albanians, like Serbs, after all, especially in that area --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. "It is a well-known fact" certainly indicates that we are about to get a leading question. Perhaps the accused could rephrase his question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Avoid leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a leading question in relation to the facts. It has to do something with a situation there, if I can put it that way. I wanted to say that it is well known that Albanians and Serbs living in that part of the world like weapons. So I wanted to ask the witness whether they organised -- was the surrender of weapons that they had received from the KLA or the collection of any kind of weapon that any one of the villagers had in their house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can give an answer to that. When I asked them to surrender their weapons, I told them to surrender those weapons which they had procured from the terrorists, because 80 per cent of the Albanians have always had a weapon. I myself was in prison some 20 times because I had kept hidden weapons. Therefore, I told those persons that whoever had a rifle, a weapon, a pistol which they had kept at home to protect themselves, not to fight the state or for terrorist purposes, I told them to surrender those weapons that they had procured from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, may I ask you to explain or clarify what is in the transcript; that you were in prison some 20 times because you kept hidden weapons. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As many as 20 times you were imprisoned for having hidden weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe not 20 times but maybe 10 times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, could you explain this? As far as I understood you, you asked them to hand over the weapons that they had received from the KLA. You did not ask them to surrender the weapons that they themselves had. Did I understand you correctly or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that if they had some weapons that they had had for many years that they had bought, whatever, that they could keep those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The state never permitted us to keep weapons with -- with permissions. We Albanians had always problems among themselves -- ourselves for petty offences for lands, for livestock, things like this, and we could buy a weapon up to 4.000 marks. And I told them not to surrender that kind of weapon which they had to protect themselves, and they didn't surrender such kind of weapons. But the state never arrest the people for holding such kind of weapons, because they knew that even if they had a rifle, they would use it only to protect themselves and not to use it against the state, for nothing else. We back then to surrender the weapons they had brought from abroad, those weapons which were used for terrorist purposes, and they did surrender those weapons. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a short while ago that you were in prison about ten times because of possession of weapons. I assume that you did not have a permit. Could you explain that in greater detail. When was it you were in prison and how much time did you spend in prison because of such violations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: From 1975 was the first time when I went to prison, when the militiamen found a pistol in my home and they sentenced me to one or two months. After that, I purchased another pistol, and this went on. I asked the state to give me a permit to hold a weapon. They didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the total? I know it's hard for you to give us an exact figure now, but what was the total time you spent in prison due to these various violations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't think I spent more than a year and a half. The greatest sentence I received was one year and a half. I apologise for starting to speak in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time when you were penalised for possessing weapons, you said that the police found a pistol in your possession and you were punished. Who were the policemen concerned; Serbs or Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on other occasions - you say that on about ten different occasions you were imprisoned for illegal possession of weapons - were the policemen who found those weapons in your possession Serbs or Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The policemen were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to this event in 1992. How many weapons did you collect during that drive, the weapons the villagers had received from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: In our village, in Osek, we didn't count every single weapon. I know that there were two tractors full of weapons. They had pistols. I know that there was also a cannon. There was -- there were all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about pistols. Were there any rifles?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I said everything from pistols to other weapons. There was also a cannon. There were automatic rifles, mortars, all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. Is it in 1992 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ibraj, you collected those weapons. What did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I took two other persons with me, and we transported these weapons to the SUP in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were the weapons different from the kind of weapons which you said earlier the Albanians kept for their protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, there were two tractors full of -- full of weapons, and all of them were new weapons. They were not old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, be so kind as to explain to us, Mr. Ibraj, whether the police or the army or any other authority whatsoever come into any sort of clash with your villagers. Was anybody punished for possession of weapons? Did the possession of weapons have any consequence for the villagers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: In Osek, there were, I think, three persons who did not surrender their weapons. They fled the village with their weapons, and they were captured by the police and condemned. Three people. The others who surrendered their weapons were not touched. They were allowed to be free and to mind their own business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police come to your village after that? Did they conduct searches, anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The police did not come to our village, because I and Mihil Abazi were there, responsible for that. When the militia had anything to do with them, they told us. The militia didn't have anything to do with our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that nobody touched the villagers throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: From the wartime up to the 14th of June, 1999, we didn't have any problems. There were some minor problems with the army forces when they were in our village, but we resolved it that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ibraj, how far is your village from the centre of Djakovica, from the town of Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: It is five kilometres away from the centre of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us sum up, then: Sometime in mid-1998, you collected the weapons. You turned them over to the SUP, and the police never came to your village again, nor did they have anything to do with the villagers. You as local security took care of maintaining law and order in the village, and there were no conflicts. Would that be the summary of what you have told us so far?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The police came to our village once. They told us to search some families that had not turned over their weapons, and I told them that I couldn't do that. They couldn't come to our village without our permission. I allowed them to come. They went and fetched that person, they took him to prison, and I don't know what happened to him after that. They took away his weapons. There was no other problem after that in our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time during the war did any of the people in your village suffer any maltreatment from the army, the police, anybody who was in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Only one family had problems with two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, may I ask you to explain your statement that the police could not come to your village without your permission. Does that relate to a specific incident or are you speaking generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general. I'm talking in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that the police had to get your permission before they could come to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wish to remind you that I explained earlier on that the Albanians had taken over security matters in a great number of villages and had an understanding with the police that they would take care of maintaining law and order themselves so that the police did not enter those villages at all, because that was the understanding between the police and a great number of villages. And that was the case with the municipality of Djakovica, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me hear from Mr. Ibraj. This was an understanding. Was it a written understanding or just an informal understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did this through the chairman of the municipality. The chairman of the municipality guaranteed us that we would have no problems whatsoever from the army or from the police. And we guaranteed the police and the army that I would be responsible for everything that might occur in my village and that on my part I guaranteed the villagers that I would be responsible for any problems that might come up with the police or the army. And this was how things went up to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you mentioned an incident that happened between one villager and two soldiers. Could you explain what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I cannot mention the name because it's not a good thing to mention someone's name here. A villager came to me in the morning and told me that two soldiers had come and asked him to give them some water. The army forces were deployed in a village in the vicinity -- in the mountain, excuse me, in the vicinity of the village, and his house was situated nearby the army place. They had asked him for water, he had given them water, and then they asked him to give them a coffee, and he gave them coffee as well. They had entered his house without the owner's permission. I wasn't there to see with my own eyes what happened, but he told me that they had taken his wife and entered another room. The other members of the family, they had asked them to stay in another room. After three or four hours, they had left the house, and he came to me crying and told me what had happened. I took him with me, this person, and went to the commune, to the municipality chairman, and woke him from sleep, because, as I said, it was very early morning and he was still sleeping. I recounted to him what I had heard from this person, and together we went to SUP, to the chief of the SUP, and asked -- and told him, "This is what has happened, and you have guaranteed me that no harm would come to our village." He told me, "Go back to the village, and in two hours we will be there." And in an hour, actually, they came. They were policemen. And they took me and went together to that person who had reported the case to me. And together with this person, we went to the army forces, and he recognised those two soldiers who were at his house, and the soldiers were taken away immediately. I don't know where they were taken and what happened to them because I remained in the village. After two or three days -- or three days, the person to whom that had happened received a note telling him that those two soldiers were sentenced in Prizren, one to six and the other to seven years of gaol. And after that, there was no other problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know what offence they were charged with, the soldiers who were sentenced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That villager, I think, said that his wife was raped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was only two or three days after. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to a different subject, but before that, let me ask you: Apart from that incident that you described as a result of which you intervened personally, whereupon the police removed the two soldiers from the area to which your village belongs, were there any other incidents? For the entire duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, there were no other incidents from the army or from the police. There was actually an incident regarding myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be so kind as to tell us briefly what kind of incident that was.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: A police car was going to Decan, and it stopped at my house, and someone told me that, "We saw a KLA group in your village." I took some local police with me and went in the direction that these policemen told me they had seen the KLA group. I went to a house, and the owner came out and I asked him whether there was someone in his house, apart from his family members, that is. He said no. And then I told him that some policemen had informed me that there were KLA members. And I said, "It's better not to create problems for the village, because I have guaranteed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them, the police, that there would be no problems here." He said, "No, there is nobody in my home and there is a group in the other house." I went to this other house and I called the owner, who came out after my call, and I asked him whether he had other people in his home, because I had news that he had, and he said no, and he started to curse me. In front of his door I saw some pair of shoes, and I guessed that there were people there. I said, "I want -- I want to go inside and search." At that moment, I didn't have any weapons on me. I don't remember even now whom I borrowed a weapon from when I entered inside. When I went into the room, I saw ten people there. I told them to stand up against the wall, and they did so. I asked them to show me their identity papers. The owner told me that he himself had their identity papers in another room, he said, and then he went to fetch them. When he came back, he attacked me. During that confrontation, two other people assaulted me from my back. I killed the owner, who was in front of me. When he fell on the ground, the others who were behind my back, when I turned, they surrendered. And then in the meantime, some other forces came to my rescue, and we arrested the other eight persons who were still alive and surrendered them to SUP. Before coming out of that house, of that room, I informed the observers who came. When they came, I don't remember well, but I think there was an Italian with them, and the investigating judge also came to the site of the event. They came and they examined the site. The investigating judge interrogated me. I don't know to this date who that person -- that judge was. I know that he came from the Peja first instance court. He gave me a verdict, a decision for self-defence. The other persons were handed over to SUP. They were from Klina, from Burasac [phoen], Kosare, and from another place I don't remember, from where two or three other persons were. Other than that, there was no other problem in the village up to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Ibraj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment I met them they were not armed and were not dressed in uniforms. They were dressed in civilian clothes. I felt embarrassed because they were -- some were from my village, and they wanted the police to come and search the family, and I didn't allow the police to come inside and search for weapons. I personally attended the funeral of the person I killed, and we observed the mourning rites for ten days, and I took care of his family as if it were my family until the end of the war. His father had a weapon, a pistol, even from before, and I didn't allow the police to take away that pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, before we move on, tell me, when you arrived at that house where the incident took place, were you accompanied by somebody else from the local security?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were alone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. Ten local policemen were there. Immediately after I was told that a KLA group had entered the village, of course I wasn't able to go there myself, so I called for others to come with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those persons you invited to accompany you, were they from the Secretariat of the Interior - in other words, the state police - or were they also local security men, Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, they were Albanians from the local defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The policemen from SUP came later, after I called them, after everything was finished. An hour later. I called for the observers and SUP members, and they came later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you have explained that for the entire duration of the war the village was peaceful, there were no KLA members. The men you described a moment ago were from Klina, as you said, not from other places. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: They were persons from Klina, Punacec [phoen], Kosare, and I don't remember all the places they came from, but I don't think there was any from my village except for the owner of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now, since I understand correctly as saying there were no KLA units in your village, let me ask you now: Were there any KLA members elsewhere who were natives of your village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Twenty-eight persons from my village were members of the KLA, persons who lived in my village. They were not KLA in my village, but they were members in other villages. They were with the KLA. I called their families, and I told their parents: "I guaranteed for this village, so you either bring your child, your son, back home or tell him not to come here in the village in a uniform and cause problems." Their parents guaranteed, and those who were members of the KLA from my village, they did not enter the village until the end of the war. And their families lived well in our village. We helped them with everything we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, apart from this collaboration which functioned very well, as we can see, with the authorities, was there any cooperation of some other kind with the authorities, such as assistance in everyday matters? How did that cooperation work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: When the war began, people became scared. They didn't feel free to go to the town and do their business. I went to the president of the municipality and asked him what to do. I told him that the villagers didn't have flour, didn't have oil. We opened a Red Cross point in a week and organised two persons, and they made up a list for every house, what each house needed, and within three days the president of municipality brought the stuff needed to me, and then we distributed them to the villagers. This aid was from Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, apart from this particular occasion when you called in the observers after that incident, did the OSCE observer mission come at all? Did its individual members come?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the observers were the first to come. After they came, I informed the police as well, and the police then came as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that incident any more. You've already described that incident. Now I'm asking you whether the OSCE observer mission came to your village. Did any members come on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Even before this incident, and after this incident, observers came to our village. But from those that came, I remember one. He was Italian. I don't remember his name. And on several occasions the chief of the observers - that's how he presented himself - he came as well; Walker. I remembered his name because he came to me and told me that his father was born in 1920, he asked for his ID card and wanted to know if he was the person. He gave him the ID card and said to him, "You raped two females, minors."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that to your father?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Walker, William Walker. I was present when he said these words to my father. And I said to him, "How can you say these words to a person who is 80 years old?" He said to me that two females had given a statement about this, so he went to fetch these two females because he saw that the person they accused was 80 years old. When these two females came, they got out of the car, and then he asked them, "Is this the person?" They said no. He then apologised, and I said to him, "How on earth can you tell an 80-year-old person -- how on earth can you accuse an 80-year-old person of raping two minor females?" I cursed him and told him that I didn't want to see him again in my village. So he left and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Ibraj, that you remembered an Italian and William Walker from all the observers. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, since Walker accused your father that time and left, how many times had you seen him before that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I had seen him before this incident and also after this incident, but I never spoke with him again. I could see him every night going to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he go to Glodjane every evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Because there was the KLA staff, and every night between, 11.00 and 12.00 p.m,. he would go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this incident did you have any conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: He came on several occasions to my house and asked me about the uniforms we wore, who these uniforms belonged to. So I explained to him that this was the uniform of the local defence. Then he asked me who gave us those uniforms, so I said to him it was Serbia who gave us these uniforms, and he said to me, "There's no longer a Serbia here." He had a band on his left arm, and the American flag as well, and he said to me, "Now you can put this flag on your uniform because there is no longer a Serbia here." And I said to him, "Go to your country, to America, and I don't want to see you again." And he never came to my house again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen, Mr. Ibraj? Can you remember, at least roughly, when it was that Walker came to your home and when it was that he said you should place an American flag there and that it was no longer Serbia? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but this happened sometime in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try, nevertheless, to remember. It was impossible for him to be there in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has given his response to the question, now the accused cannot be putting words into the witness's mouth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, that's not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date. As I said earlier, I had many problems and have problems to this date. I don't know the exact date. Now, whether it was 1998 or 1999, I don't know, but I know that it was before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I was trying to help the witness remember, try to remember in order to get to that date, because the witness had already apologised that he cannot remember the date because he had a great many problems, which we will see, major problems at that. And since he already gave his apology stating that he could not remember the date, I was just trying to help him, or, rather, I just asked him what time this was, and I was just telling him it could not have been in May 1998, of course. But never mind. Never mind. After all, never mind. He explained to us now it was before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say May 1998. I didn't say May 1998. I said it could be in May 1998, or beginning of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the bombing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the bombing, were there any effects of the NATO bombing in your village itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: There were no damages in the village except for the schoolyard where they threw some --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was there in the schoolyard? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: There was no damage to the school itself or to the people but only to the yard. Some bombs were thrown in the yard. The army was stationed in the mountains near the school, so they were bombing them in the vicinity of the school, but the school itself, the school building was outside the village. It was not in the village. They threw cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which army do you say was based in the mountains near the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian army, part of Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put a few questions to you, and I'm going to quote what it says in 63, 66, 86, and 87. I want to apologise in advance. These quotations are rather lengthy. The interpretation takes place into Albanian and then into Serbian, so it takes awhile. Just tell me one thing: The army of Yugoslavia and the police of Serbia, did they ever expel citizens from your village or Djakovica? Did they ever make them leave their villages in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the basis that this question has been framed to encompass all of the villages in Kosovo and Metohija, not just the villages -- the village where this witness lived and worked, and I don't see how this witness then can possibly respond to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he may have information. Let us hear the answer. Let's deal with your village first, Mr. Ibraj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No violence was exercised against my village by the KLA or the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us deal specifically with the question of expelling people from your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody from my village fled the village. Nobody left. Everyone was in the village until I left, until 14th of June, 1999. They carried on their normal work. Nobody left for Albania. Not a single house was burnt. They lived their life normally, as if there was no war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say what happened in relation to other villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for other villages, all the information I have is from hearsay and from what I've seen on television. Every village had local police, and every local police was in charge of its own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, do you know that a great many Albanians went to Macedonia and Albania during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: This is something that everybody knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the authorities, the police or the military, forcing Albanians to go to Albania or Macedonia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the police and the army actually returned them back to their homes. They wouldn't let them go. There was a case when a truck loaded with people stopped near me and asked for water. I asked them where they were heading to, they said they were going to Albania. I asked them, "Why you're going to Albania?" and they answered to me, "Well, we have to leave Kosova because Kosova is being bombed by NATO, and we are leaving because of the bombing." This is to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you were in your own village. Since it is, as you said, five kilometres away from the centre of Djakovica, tell me, during the war, or generally speaking on the eve of the war, did you go to Djakovica often or were you in your own village only?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I went also to Gjakove. My office was in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were in Djakovica every day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Up to the bombing I was in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the bombing started, how often did you go to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Only when I had to go and see the president of municipality for a short meeting, because there was heavy bombing in Gjakove and we were afraid to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a way, since you were five kilometres away from the centre and since you came to see the president of the municipality and to attend these meetings, were you aware of the situation in Djakovica apart from what you've already said, that it was heavily bombed? Were you aware of the situation in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: To my opinion, Gjakove was bombed the most. The factory was one kilometre far from my house, and when they bombed this factory, two or three persons died from shock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to read what I've already told you that I would read, and then you're going to tell me, since you were in Djakovica at the time, whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 63(h), 63(h). And also the subparagraphs of paragraph (h). They pertain to Djakovica specifically where Mr. Ibraj was head of the local security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Surely you can summarise and put questions of fact to him based on that. Do we have to suffer your reading on two pages of the indictment? Put to him the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if this is the substance, it says here that from the 24th of March, 1999, onwards, or around that date, and all the way up to the 11th of May, 1999, that is to say from the beginning of the bombing on the 24th of March until the 11th of May, so that's about six or seven weeks, that forces of the FRY and Serbia were forcing the citizens of the town of Djakovica to leave their homes, that they went from house to house and called upon Albanians to move out, and that practically they were expelling Albanians from Djakovica, forcing them to go to Macedonia, Albania -- never mind where; they were basically expelling them from Kosovo. Is that correct, Mr. Ibraj?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: As far as Gjakove is concerned, to my knowledge only those who the police and the army could not prevent from going, they left. Otherwise, nobody forced them to leave Gjakove. Not the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, what is stated here goes beyond that. It says that in many cases the military and the police were forcing the Albanians out of their homes and forcing them to go, and they say in some cases people were killed and many were threatened with death. Many shops and homes that belonged to Albanians from Kosovo were torched while Serb premises were protected. Tell me now, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: How many times shall I repeat this? As I said to you, I never heard that the police or the army told someone to leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In Ibraj, let me clarify one thing. During the war, you stayed mostly in your village, Osek Hilja. Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one thing about what Mr. Kwon asked you. You were head of the local security. Is that not correct, Mr. Ibraj?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: For Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Kwon, Mr. Ibraj took care of his village but he was head of local security for all of Djakovica. As he explained, he was in Djakovica very often. Practically, he is aware of what was going on in Djakovica throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness give the evidence, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that he was in local police for his village. Mr. Ibraj, you are the local police or defence for Gjakove village or Osek Hilja village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the local defence for Osek village but was chief of the local defence in the level of Gjakove municipality. In other words, I had a group of 17 persons, members of the local defence, and I was chief of these 17 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Drawn from where, the 17 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 17 persons were working for the local defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Local defence for Osek Hilja village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I and Mihil Abazi were the two persons of the local defence for Osek Hilja village. There were three persons for Osek Pasa village, two for Qerim village, two for Trakanic village, Lower Novoselle village two persons, two for Piskote village, two for Qerim village. So in other words, I was chief of this group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So those villages constitute upper part of Djakovica, northern part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me understand one more geographic matter. You once said that you once worked at Erenik village. How near is it from Gjakove, because I couldn't find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is situated between Gjakove and Osek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Osek Hilja or Pasa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between Osek Hilja and Osek Pasa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing: There is a river called Erenik in Gjakove, but I refer to the agricultural enterprise Erenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it must be very near from Qerim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, I would like us to clear up one issue. Since you were at the head of the local security of Djakovica, were you aware of the situation in Djakovica as a whole or did you only know about your village, Osek Hilja?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I was in charge of the Osek village and I can say -- I can tell you also what I know about Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking what you know about Djakovica. You will tell me whether you know certain things or you don't. For instance, in this paragraph which I summarised, it also says, among other things, that on the 24th of March the old mosque in Rogovo, a historical centre in Djakovica, which included a bazaar, a mosque, and an Islamic library, it says that there were several cultural facilities which were destroyed in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whole or in part, and it says it was done on the 24th of March by the Serbian army and the police. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The mosque in Odun [phoen] was bombed by the NATO. The police station was also bombed by the NATO. The fruit juice factory was also bombed by the NATO. The bazaar, too, including the traffic lights until the Catholic church, was also bombed by the NATO. This is all I know about Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that someone from our army or the police torched houses and destroyed buildings in Djakovica without you knowing it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. I don't know of anything like this. If the police had done so in Gjakove, then I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ibraj. Let us look now at a couple of other points from paragraph 66. It's very brief, and I will quote. It says 66(e) or, rather, (i): "On or about the early morning hours of 27th of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia came to Grezda. Women were ordered to go to an upper floor." It's 66(e): "On or about the evening of the 26th of March, 1999, in the town of Gjakove, forces of the FRY and Serbia came to a house at 134a Ymer Grezda Street. The women and children inside the house were separated from the men, and were ordered to go upstairs. The forces of the FRY and Serbia then shot and killed the six Kosovo Albanian men who were in the house. (The names of those killed are set forth in Schedule D...)" Do you know anything about those six Albanians killed at this address?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I've just heard about this question only now. I was not aware of this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can neither confirm nor deny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not heard about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But since it happened, according to this paragraph, on the eve of the 26th of March, 1999, did you -- would you have to know about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I've not heard about this incident. I don't know what to reply about this question, because I don't know anything about it. I've not heard about these killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of these names that I read out to you: Sylejman Begolli, Arif Bytyqi, Urim Bytyqi, Emin Dervishdana, Fahri Dervishdana, Zenel Dervishdana, the people listed as killed in this incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I have known the first Dervishdana. He is from Dusina. He is not from Gjakove. As for the rest, I don't know them. I have not heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will now read to you what it says in paragraph (h), 66(h). Qerim district is mentioned here. It says: "On or about the late evening of the 1st of April, 1999, and continuing through the early morning hours of the 2nd of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched an operation against the Qerim district of Djakovica. Over a period of several hours, forces of the FRY and Serbia forcibly entered the houses of Kosovo Albanians in the Qerim district, killed the occupants, and then set fire to the buildings. Dozens of homes were destroyed and over 50 persons were killed. For example, in a house located at 157 Milos Gilic Street, forces of the FRY and Serbia shot the occupants and then set the house on fire. As a result of the shootings and the fires set by the forces of the FRY and Serbia at this single location, 20 Kosovo Albanians were killed, of whom 19 were women and children. (The names ... are set out in Schedule D -- G...)" I will now read out to you those names from Schedule G: Dalina Caka, Delvina Caka, Diona Caka, Valbona Caka, Hysen Gashi, Doruntina Haxhiavdija, Egzon Haxhiavdija, Rina Haxhiavdija, Valbona Haxhiavdija, Flaka Hoxha, Shahindere Hoxha, Manushe Nuci, Shirine Nuci, Arlind Vejsa, Dorina Vejsa, Fetije Vejsa, Marigona Vejsa, Rita Fejsa, Sihana Vejsa, Tringa Vejsa. These are the names on the list related to this incident that allegedly happened in Qerim involving the death of over 50 persons, as it says, in the evening of the 1st of April and in the morning of the 2nd of April. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The village of Qerim is very far away from my village. As refers to the question you asked me, this is not true at all. In the village of Qerim, none of the houses was killed during the war. They were neither destroyed nor razed to the ground. From what I have heard, they are -- they are Muslim names. No family -- in the village of Qerim, all the people are Catholic. None of them is Muslim. In the village of Qerim, there is only one house that belongs to a Serb, and before the bombing this house was destroyed. There was no other house in Qerim village that was destroyed, neither there are there any Muslims. All the people belonged to the Catholic religion. So as regards the question, what you said, it is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you mentioned also some members of the local security who answered to you but were in charge of Qerim. Is that the same locality or is that a different one?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. We're talking about this, about Qerim, this locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We heard a witness here by the name of Bec Beqaj from Djakovica. He stated that in August 1998, the population of Racaj and other villages left the village for the first time when the army arrived in that area. And on the 14th of April, 1999, the police and the army came again to Racaj and ordered the villagers to leave their homes. Do you know anything about the area of the village of Racaj, and would you say that this witness Bec Beqaj was correct in saying that the police and the army ordered the population of Racaj to leave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I know where the village of Racaj is located. My wife comes from this village. Bec Beqaj is my brother-in-law, but what he stated is not true. The police and the army did not evict the people from this village, but they had an order from terrorists to leave the villages as they were told that the NATO was going to bomb them, and then we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say Bec Beqaj is your brother-in-law. You know him, and what he stated is not true. Do you know of any reason why he would lie?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Well, probably he did not dare to say that KLA told us to leave the village, and we should say that the police told us to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, what is the basis for your saying that they had an order from terrorists to leave the village as they were told that NATO was going to bomb them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they did not go from my village to go to Albania or to any other place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm seeking to find out is the basis for the knowledge that you had. How did you -- how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because the head of the municipality told me that neither the police nor the army can touch us, and they assured me that the people are safe from the police and the army, and we are not going anywhere. I assured them that I will protect them from the army and the police as the KLA did not dare enter our village, and that's why the people did not leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you have answered my question, which was: How did you come to know that terrorists told them to leave the villages as NATO was going to bomb them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they went to someone and told him to give the order, because they could not go from every house, from house to house. They just told one person to tell the other villagers to leave. And then this person spread the news in the village. There were cases when the people were asked, "Why are you leaving? Why are you leaving the village?" "We do not dare do this because of the KLA. We have an order from the KLA to leave the village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear that in person, Mr. Ibraj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Zujo Hamza from the village of Repaj [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we were talking about village of Racaj. You said the people in Racaj were told from the KLA to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Without considering the village of Racaj, every village had to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the furthest I can get. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you mentioned a moment ago that somebody from the KLA would convey a message to one person in the village and give KLA orders this way rather than go from house to house. How did it normally function? To whom would this order be given and how would it be enforced if it is told to only one person in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: This was, so to say, organised step-by-step, from the lowest -- from the lowest person in authority up to the commander. I had one person in my village. His name was Afrim Ljulji. I protected his family in the village, and he was a key person for the KLA. And in this area, he was the person who had to give announcements and had to accompany the KLA in the village, convey the messages. I took the example of Afrim Ljulji, but there were many like him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you answer that other part of my question? If something is conveyed to one person in the village, who does that person have to be so that the entire village should listen to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: There was one occasion in my village where some villager, old people, came and told me that Afrim Ljulji told us to leave the village. What are you telling us? And I told them stay, don't leave. Don't worry. But they refused to do so. Somewhere somebody was scared to do so. Somebody followed the order. The -- the entire village helped me. They were on my side, because I alone could not have been able to do so. All the villagers helped me and supported me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Another witness testified here, Nike Peraj. He stated that in April 1999, the KLA killed Milutin Prascevic, who was head of the MUP in Djakovica, plus another four officers, after which, on the 27th and the 28th of April, Serb forces started a major operation in a valley to the north of Djakovica. Do you know anything about what was going on in Djakovica at that time, and did you hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I have known Nike Peraj. He was an officer in the Serbian army, first class captain. I've also known Milutin Prascevic. He was not an army -- a police officer, but he was a simple policeman. I heard when he was killed there was another Albanian who was killed along with him, and he was also a policeman, an ordinary policeman. His name was Naser Arifaj. Nike Peraj comes from the village of Ramoc. His son was a member of the KLA. His brother was a KLA commander. For Ramoc. He came to me -- there was one occasion when he came to me and told me that my father was sick, because his father was an old man, and he asked me to offer him a kind of a local protection and escort him to go and see his father in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ramoc. I told him, "You are an army officer. Why do you need my protection? Why do you need me to protect you? You can take 20 soldiers and go there." He said, "No, I'm not scared from the police or army, but I'm scared of the KLA to go there." And then I gave him three members of the local defence, and they escorted him by car. He went to the house, he saw his father, he stayed one hour with him father, and then he came back. This is all I know about this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read out to you just one paragraph of his statement which mentions your village, Osek Hilja. It also mentions Osek Pasa in Djakovica municipality. He says: "Belgrade decided that each municipality should have a police unit consisting of loyal Albanians, loyal to Serbia. They sent them to maintain security in villages where the atmosphere was too hostile for other policemen to work. In those villages, they collected intelligence for the Serbian police about the local population. That started in the summer of 1998. Such a group existed in Osek Hilja and Osek Pasa in Djakovica. There was a father there with two sons, and there was a group of 20 men led by Hila Abazi. This father was Muharem Musa Jakupi. He had two wives and had 70 something years. The youngest son did not want to join the police, and he was beaten up. One of the sons was called Sahid, whereas his brother was the leader of that family group and also a bodyguard of Momcilo Stanojevic. The eldest son was the only one who wore a camouflage uniform, and the others wore blue uniforms with pointed caps, normal for the regular police. He also says that in the Djakovica area there were two policemen only of the local MUP and their commander was Milutin Prascevic, who was later killed in Meja." So this was a paragraph from this statement. I also mentioned to you the testimony of Nike Peraj. Tell me, did this village have local security because they were too hostile to Serbs or for some other reason? Because it says here they sent them to maintain order in these villages because the atmosphere was too hostile to Serbia for other policemen to work there. Is that the real reason?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The local security was set up in Gjakove by Momcilo Stanojevic, who was head of the municipality at the time. What Belgrade decided, I don't know, and this was something I was not interested in. Where the local police or the local security worked, there were no damages, neither in Serbs nor in Albanians. As for the witness -- as for the statement of Nike Peraj, he gave this statement because of his son, because his son would have killed him if he had not given that false statement, because until the end of the war he worked in the Serbian army. Wherever the local police worked or operated, this was a protected area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you what it is in Peraj's statement that you say was false.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing stated in that statement is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, for example, when he says that the KLA killed Milutin Prascevic, who was head of the MUP, plus another four officers, that's not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Prascevic was killed but he was not head of MUP. He was an ordinary policeman. The four others, they weren't officers. They were local policemen. One of them was Albanian, and the three others were ordinary policemen. It is true that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not known who killed them, but most probably the KLA, because the KLA was nearby in the mountains. And they fired from the mountain with a hand-held rocket launcher. They fired at them and killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Xhevahire Syla, another witness, stated that on the 14th of April, mixed Serbian forces entered Nivokaz, the municipality of Djakovica. They entered Albanian houses and gave people five minutes to leave them. That's how a convoy was established that went towards Djakovica. The police attacked some people in the convoy and told them to go to Albania and that refugees were not allowed to leave the route along which they were moving to Prizren and which was a road leading to the border, and that's where the convoy was stopped, near the Bistrica [as interpreted] bridge. The Serb forces separated from the convoy and the convoy was later hit by a NATO bomb, and after that three low-flying aircraft carrying Serb flags flew over their heads and bombed the convoy seven times and killed 70 to 80 people. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Either I didn't understand the question or you didn't explain it well. I don't know where Bistrica bridge is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Bistrazin is the bridge. I am sorry if this was too long, but I quoted this to you. I told you what Xhevahire Syla, a witness here, said, and I'm telling you what she claimed. She testified on the 17th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, the transcript page is 8186.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us take things in order. She said that Serb forces entered Nivokaz. Do you know that village in the municipality of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I know this village, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And it says that the Serb forces came and entered houses, giving people five minutes to leave their homes. That is how this convoy was established. And police attacked people in this convoy, telling them to go to Albania, and then they went to Prizren. Let's stop at that point. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I know where Nivokaz village is. It is three kilometres from the border with Albania. The village of Bistrazin is about seven or eight kilometres far from Gjakove. I'm surprised how this person could give this statement. How can police or army pursue someone? Because it's only six kilometres from Nivokaz and Gjakove. And from Gjakove to Bistrazin another seven kilometres. So I don't know why they were heading to Bistrazin and in the direction of Prizren in order to get to Albania. It's about 100 kilometres longer journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the distance from Nivokaz and the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Nivokaz is three or four kilometres far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think this is sufficient. I'm not even going to ask you about the bombing of refugees. Actually, Merfidete Selmani testified here, and she stated that on the 14th of April, 1999, the Serb soldiers entered the village of Dobroz and that led to the flight of the population. When they passed Djakovica and got close to the Bistrazin bridge, then she heard an explosion and she saw smoke coming from parts of the convoy going in front of her. And what happened? Serb soldiers entered the village of Dobroz, expelled the population, and then when they passed Djakovica, then what happened happened in Bistrazin. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about this. This is not clear to me, and I cannot give you any answer to this question. Dobroz is five kilometres away from Gjakove, and it is close to the border with Albania, and neither the police or army could go to these areas, mountainous areas, to force these people out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one question in relation to that. These witnesses say that these convoys from these villages, Nivokaz, Dobroz, had to go through Djakovica in order to go towards Prizren. Would people notice such convoys in Djakovica if they were passing through Djakovica? Djakovica's a big town, or a relatively big town. Did anything happen? Did the military and the police force a convoy through Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't think that the police or army forced them out. And even if that was the case, the border with Albania was very close. From Nivokaz to Bistrazin there are only five kilometres between. And if they passed through Gjakove, someone would have seen them, such a long convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to put a few more questions to you now. One general question: Actually, paragraph 87 here reads as follows, since you yourself said that you lived in Kosovo, in Djakovica all the time, for a while you were in the service, it reads as follows: "After adopting the new constitution of Serbia on the 28th of September, 1990 --" oh, no. Sorry, sorry. No, sorry. 87: "After Kosovo's autonomy was practically abolished, in Kosovo there were increasing political divisions. At the end of 1990 --" please bear the dates in mind, the end of 1990 -- "and throughout 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanians, physicians, teachers, workers, policemen, and state employees were dismissed from their jobs." Tell me, please, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they did not expel them from work. Only those who wanted to leave their jobs, only they left their jobs. Albanians were employed in the police and in every enterprise they wanted to work until the end of the war, but Albanians who refused to leave their jobs, they were warned by the KLA. They were told either to leave their jobs or -- I'll give you an example. My father was followed. His activities were followed. So he was told by the KLA, "You either become one of us or we will kill you." So Albanians who did not abandon their jobs from the 1990s onwards, their families suffered either kidnappings or killings or their houses were destroyed or they were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the KLA as a structured body exist in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't a public knowledge. They operated secretly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to put you questions that have to do with your family only, Mr. Ibraj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I put these questions, gentlemen, I would like to draw your attention to the following. Today -- here's the date, the 17th of August, 2005 -- I just got it from Professor Rakic, I received disclosure of the [In English] "Rule 68 material related to Kosovo and Defence witness Muharem Ibraj." [Interpretation] So this is a statement that was taken from this witness on the 13th of May, 2002. It was submitted to me today, on the day of the witness's testimony. I just said that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to your family. Some of this is contained in this statement, too, the statement that they took from you. You had some personal losses in your family. Please tell us about it, Mr. Ibraj.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Until June 1999, I defended my village and the villages around as much as I could. I helped them with humanitarian aid, but I was also helped by the people. In June 1999, I had to leave Kosova. After KFOR came to Kosova, six members of my family were kidnapped; my three brothers, my son, and two sons of my brother. When I found out about this, I informed the International Red Cross, I informed the KFOR, and I reported everywhere I could, but ever since I have no knowledge on their whereabouts. I know who the people who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. took them are, and these people who kidnapped my brothers are still free. One of them is even here in Holland. He's been here for five years now. When I made some inquiries why this befell on me, the answer was, "Because you did not cooperate with them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, that and what it says here in the statement that you gave in 2002 or, rather, it says here -- well, I haven't got any page numbers here, unfortunately. It should be page 4, I think. It's what I got today: "[In Englishj] After his return to his village Osek Hilja, about one week after he had been kidnapped for the first time, two person took Ibr Ibraj; one was his cousins Djavit Ibraj from Osek Hilja, and a person with name Isni Bunjoki from the village Racaj. I know that Ibr, who was also working as a village security officer in Skiljanje once before arrested his cousin Xhavit when he was with a gun, pulled his ear and forced him to leave the village. This time Ibr was taken to the UCK headquarter in Junik and he was never seen again."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then says: "[In English] When my son Kujtim Ibraj was taken away by the UCK, he was together with Isa Ibraj and a person with name Ram Ademaj. Ademaj was released one day later, while my son Kujtim and Isa Ibraj are still missing."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: This is a mistake because my brother and my son were taken by Ram Ademaj. Ram Ademaj was not arrested with my brother and my son but was the person who took them. He is in his house now, but as for my brother and son, I still don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time has gone by since your family members were abducted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: They were kidnapped on 18th of June, 1999. Between 18th of June and 26th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that it's been six years now since they've been abducted.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it's been more than six years now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were abducted between the 18th and --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: 25th of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's at the time when KFOR was in charge of safety and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to have the copies of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After they kidnapped them, they burnt down their houses, they expelled their wives and children from their homes, and from that day on we have been scattered all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, thank you very much for your testimony. I'm just going to ask for you to comment upon this document that we've provided here as an exhibit. This is a letter sent to you by the KLA. Could it please be given to the witness so that he could briefly say what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: This letter, in the beginning of 1998, I found it in the street just in front of my house, together with five Albanian leks wrapped in the letter. I read this letter --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five Albanian what? I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Five Albanian currency, lek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpretation was "leg," "five legs," so I didn't understand what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. The Albanian currency is called lek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I understand how come the mistake was made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
