utterances.text: The meaning of these five leks was that you have a deadline, until you spend all these five leks, to live. I didn't know to whom I should write a response, but I answered to myself and my family. I thought that I should not be against one state, and the KLA in this case was not the state. I didn't want to be against the state and join the KLA. Eventually the content of this letter came true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please admit this into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear, Mr. Ibraj, how was it you knew the letter was for you? Is it because of the use of a nickname rather than your own name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of my father is written on the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question: Did you have an opportunity to read this statement? In all fairness, I received it only today. I quoted just a few sentences from it to you a few moments ago, those that pertain to the members of your family, but you already said that Ram Ademaj was not arrested but that this was actually the man who kidnapped them, who took them away. Did you have the opportunity of reading this statement and did you see whether there were some other inaccurate interpretations of what you'd said, because right now I did not have the opportunity of reading all of it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, 1999, I left Kosova, but my entire family was at home. Ram Ademaj, who is my neighbour, went together with 20 KLA members to my house and took my brother and my son. My entire family was there. My family asked Ram, "Why are you doing this? What did they do to you?" And his reply was, "We will only question them and we will release them tomorrow." But they never returned, and we don't know anything about their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ibraj. Thank you for having testified. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The statement -- do you want the statement exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it could be exhibited, but after the witness reads it in his own language and checks its accuracy. As you can see, a portion that I quoted to him contains not an error but a grave mistake, a grave inaccuracy. Ram Ademaj, who took away his family, and they haven't been heard of since, the witness cannot know now what else has perhaps been misinterpreted there, and I can't tell either because I just got it. Is there any kind of procedure for the witness to read this first and then to have it admitted into evidence? I think that would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution doesn't see any grounds for this statement to be admitted into evidence. The statement was provided to Mr. Milosevic as a caution under Rule 68, because arguably the statement contains material that could be considered exculpatory to the accused, but certainly the evidence of the witness is his testimony today, not his prior statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness confirms the veracity of this statement, there is no reason to reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I think the reason -- one reason, Your Honour Judge Kwon, would be that it would go against the practice of this trial, that prior statements by witnesses, whether they're -- whether the accuracy is confirmed or not, they are -- they have not, as a rule, been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be the difference from the so-called 89(F) practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, one difference would be, Your Honour, that there was no read-back -- there was no declaration given under Rule -- you asked for 89 or Rule 92 bis, because I heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 89(F). If witnesses are given opportunity to read through their statement, if it confirms that what the content is true, and if it is relevant, I would say, speaking for myself, there would be no reason to reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, there -- I take Your Honour's point that it may be consistent with Rule 89(F) at this time. However, the witness has provided his testimony on these events. We don't see any reason then why this -- the purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a different point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The purpose of Rule 89(F) is to save time, not to pile on additional evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, I'd like to ask you why as a Kosovo Albanian you did not support the KLA, who were supposed to be fighting for your liberation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not support the KLA because the KLA was not a state. The KLA was against the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the only reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for only this reason. I didn't want to be against the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you gave an indication early in your evidence that, generally speaking, Albanians who kept weapons or a weapon, normally for protection, were simply allowed to keep it. No action was taken against them. Why was it that regularly action was taken against you for possessing a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were rare occasions. For example, a person who possessed a weapon in the past and now and was not against the state, did not steal, did not perform any illegal activities, nobody would touch him for possessing that weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I understood. So why were you touched so often for possessing your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I did not hide my weapon in my house, but I carried it with me everywhere I went, to cafeteria outside my home, and they found it in my possession and took it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why did you carry it around with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I wished to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. On a separate matter, can you tell me why you, a person who was regularly imprisoned for carrying the weapon, was chosen to head the local security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no security forces there. It was the local defence of the village. The village had no problems with me or caused by me ever. You couldn't find a better defender for the village than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean that it was up to the Albanian population of the village to choose the person who would have the responsibility of local defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And not only in my village but in every village the villagers themselves elected their leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who then decided that of the 17 people in that position, you should be in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chairman of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just one final matter, separate matter. The incident in which you killed a person also involved the apprehension of eight KLA suspects and the handing over of these suspects to the SUP. Can you tell me what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know they were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, if I can take up my colleague's question further as for your appointment. My understanding is that you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appointed by the president of municipality. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whose name is Momcilo Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that he's a Serb by his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he's a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the president of the municipality elected by the people or appointed by somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, a moment ago Mr. Robinson asked you about the reasons why you were against the KLA when the KLA was fighting for Albanian freedom. I want to ask you, through all those years, were Albanians in Kosovo not free, or was their freedom restricted and needed defending?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: To my knowledge, and I speak only on my behalf, I had no problems whatsoever. The state existed. If you got involved in politics, in thefts, robberies, the state would arrest you. One would have a job. The state would secure that job for that person. So for the good persons the state existed, and for the bad ones -- I have made some mistakes and was arrested, but I do not blame the state for these mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Saxon, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a minute ago that if you got involved in politics, in thefts, robberies, the state would arrest you. Why would the state arrest you because you got involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Because the state gets involved in it, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were still living in Kosovo during the 1990s, was it considered a bad thing to become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I was a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo. I'm going to tell you something that happened to me. During the elections, which were held in the school of our village, I went there and vote and -- got all the ID cards of all my family member, went there and voted at the school. When I came back, I found the police patrol in front of my house. They asked me, "Where have you been?" I said, "I went to vote." "Did you vote?" they asked me. I said, "Yes." They said, "For whom did you vote?" I said "Rugova." And they just smiled, and then they left and I did not have any problems. No one has -- no one has hindered us from voting, but however, to get involved in politics, these were only authorised people, because as far as I know -- what do I know about politics? Why they have not imprisoned Ibrahim Rugova because he was head of the chairman of the Democratic League of Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, I'm going to cut you off now. I think you've tried to answer my question. You said only authorised people could get involved in politics. What kind of persons were authorised to get involved in politics in Kosovo during the 1990's?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Well, for example, Ibrahim Rugova. Ibrahim Rugova was our chairman. We voted for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the power to decide who could be authorised to get involved in politics in Kosovo and who could not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what right they had or who had that right. What I know is that Ibrahim Rugova was the chairman of the Democratic League of Kosovo, for Kosova, and we voted for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- at that time during the 1990s, Kosovo was controlled by a government led by this accused; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The government of Kosovo -- the government of Kosovo, Kosovo was part of -- is still part of the Republic of Serbia, and for a long time this accused was president of the Republic of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of people that you knew who were -- besides yourself, who suffered harassment by the police because they were getting involved in politics, other Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I know a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Mr. Saxon is asking the witness since you are mistreated, were any other Albanians mistreated because they participated in the political life? The witness said he was not abused because he was politically involved. He said, in fact, he was not abused at all. He made mistakes. He's not blaming the police. And he said a moment ago that he was arrested for illegal possession of weapons, not because he was politically involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, now that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the word "harassment" is inappropriate, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has just explained how a can of petrol was left in front of his home by policemen after he became politically active. So the word harassment, with all due respect, sounds quite fair. I'll try to rephrase my question now that the accused unfortunately has again put words into the witness's mouth. Is this an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. We'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon and Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber has decided to admit the letter to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an impression that there is a problem with interpretation because it goes into Serbian through English. I understood Mr. Saxon as mentioning a can of petrol. I didn't hear the witness mentioning a can of petrol. It was also in the transcript, by the way. And he didn't talk about petrol, he talked about a police patrol that was in front of his house. So maybe we should look into what he really said and how it was interpreted. And this is not the only instance about which I have certain doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We'll look into that matter. There is a big difference, of course, between a can of petrol and a police patrol. Mr. Milosevic, it might be as well if you yourself looked into the transcript, because you have the familiarity with the language, to pick up mistakes and bring it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the LiveNote record, page 51, line 14, "police patrol."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Police patrol."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just as we understood the evidence to be as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I can be assisted by Mr. Kay with the number, because I was away. This exhibit, the Registrar said it was D361, but I couldn't follow. It should be 302 or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't been into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We could check it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from your own experience after you became involved with Mr. Rugova's party, can you tell us what happened to other persons that you knew who became politically active during the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, before the break, in response to a question from Mr. Milosevic, you mentioned that the -- if you got involved in politics, the state would arrest you, and I simply want to explore that point a little bit with you. And can you tell us, please, whether you can recall specific instances of people who were arrested because they got involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I said even before that elections were proceeded freely, were held freely. We were able to vote freely for whoever we wanted. As regards the state, the state did not prevent us from voting for Rugova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say that if you got involved in politics the state would arrest you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I cannot recall how I said it. If you get involved in politics, the state arrests you. When I -- I already said elections were held freely. I voted freely myself. I met the police patrol, and I explained what I've done, and no one told -- no one asked me anything, no one told me anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police patrol who came by your house, was that the patrol of Serb policemen or the Albanian local defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, the local defence did not exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know who sent the police patrol past your house at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The police patrol did not come directly to my house, but they were patrolling along the streets, villages, cities, and then I ran into them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I assume there is some mistake in translation in relation to the politics, so if I can clarify. Mr. Ibraj, to the question of the accused whether there was any problem in relation to your freedom or something like that, you answered like this: "To my knowledge, and I speak only on my behalf, I had no problems whatsoever. The state existed." And then you said, "If you got involved in politics, in thefts, robberies, the state would arrest you." Is it a correct interpretation of what you had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it even earlier, that I've been to prison several times myself for my mistakes. The state warned me because I was illegally -- I was in illegal possession of weapons. And not only me, but 80 per cent of Albanians were in prisons for illegal possession of weapons. They were in prison for thefts, beating, and the state -- killings, and the state imprisoned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you mentioned the politics as well for the reason the state can arrest you. Is it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know that state arrested people for being involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic. During your direct testimony, you described an incident where you killed a man in your village, and you explained how, after that incident, you called for the OSCE observers and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the SUP. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- and you explained that the observers from the OSCE came to your village, both not only at the time of that incident but before it and afterwards. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The OSCE mission, observer mission, was in Kosovo from approximately early November 1998 to around the 20th of March, 1999. Can you recall approximately when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The incident occurred sometime in -- sometime in February, mid-February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I think it was like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the name of the person who you killed that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Sulejman Bajrami.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your nickname is Mush or Musa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nickname?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: My father's name is Mush. However, everyone called him Musk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are also known in the area of your village and around Gjakove as Mush or Musk at times. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: My father, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a copy of the statement that you provided to the ICTY. Perhaps the first page, a copy could be placed on the ELMO. You'll see -- Mr. Ibraj, do you see your signature at the bottom of the first page?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your initials on that page as well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your initials on the bottom of the preceding pages? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the very last page, if you turn to the last page, it says in English "Signed," and then we see the name "Muharem Ibraj," with your initials. Is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a witness acknowledgement which says that: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Do you recall having this statement read over to you in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go back to the very first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The cover page. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cover page, you see at the top there's the last name Ibraj, and then it says first name Muharem. To the right, it says father's first name: Musta -- or Musa. And then there's a word that says nickname: Musk. That's your nickname, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. That's the nickname of my father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two comments there, Mr. Saxon. It may be that the nickname Musk relates to the father's first name, which is on the right. And secondly, would that part have been read over to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. The practice of the OTP is to read over all of the information, including the names, date of birth, et cetera, et cetera. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around Gjakove, sir, some people -- let me step back from that. Your father, his nickname then is Musk. Would he also -- is he still alive, your father?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's also known as Mush or Musa Jakupi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, around Gjakove, you are known, for example, not only by the name Muharem Ibraj but people might refer to you as Muharem Jakupi or even Mush Jakupi. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People do refer to you with the last name Jakupi because of your father. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No. Muharem Jakupi is another person. Those who do not know my last name Ibraj, they call me Muharem Muski. No one calls me by the name of Muharem Jakupi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several members of the Jakupi family were members of the local security force in your village, were they not? It's a big family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: There were only six members, six members of this family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And several of them were members of the local defence force in your village; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The local defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Several members of the Jakupi family in your village were part of the local defence unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because your father was a well-known man in the area, some people around Gjakove and in your village referred to this local defence force in Osek Hilja as the Mush Jakupi unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that in Kosovo generally, and around Gjakove in particular, you and other members of this local defence unit, the Mush Jakupi unit, had a reputation and still have a reputation for criminal violence. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you and the members of the local defence unit in the village where you were and in Gjakove have a reputation as being violent criminals? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have another document I'd like to place on the ELMO, if I could ask for the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you something. This is a chapter from the report by the OSCE called "As Seen, As Told."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's from Exhibit 106. It's in the chapter on Djakovica, pages 170 to 187. And perhaps if -- thank you. If the first page could be put on the ELMO. We see there is a section there called "The Jakupi family and 'local security arrangements.'" It says -- it begins there at the top of the first paragraph: "Djakovica municipality had its own particular 'local security arrangements.'" And there's a paragraph there that describes it. If we can turn over to the next page, please. And I'm sorry if the -- yes. Thank you very much. If we could see a little bit more of the first page, because I need to read from the top. So if the page could be moved down a bit on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see a paragraph that says: "In practice, the group was run by a traditionally 'loyal' local Kosovo Albanian clan, the 'Jakupis.'" And then in the following paragraph, sir, it says the following: "The OSCE-KVM received many reports from local Kosovo Albanians who claimed to have been ill-treated or harassed by members of the Jakupi 'security police.' They said they were threatened and beaten if they were seen talking to OSCE-KVM patrols. The OSCE-KVM also received reports that 'policemen' of this group sexually harassed women when they arrested them or invited them to the police station for interviewing." It's true then, sir, isn't it, that in the Gjakove area you and the so-called local defence force that you led had a reputation for mistreating and abusing the civilian population. Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: First of all, the Jakupi family does not exist. This is Ibraj family, my family. Second, no forces apart from local defence existed. What belongs to Jakupi family, these come from people who do not know who I am or who is a local policeman. And then probably they assume so and gave that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you acknowledged a few minutes ago that your local defence force was sometimes known as the Mush Jakupi unit. Second of all, I'm going to show you, sir, that many people knew exactly who you were and who the members of your so-called local defence force was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I ask the usher's assistance again, please. Perhaps if copies could be distributed to the other people in the courtroom, please. And if a copy could be placed on the ELMO. First the first page. This is a printout from the Internet. It's from a website of the Kosova Crisis Centre, and it's the news from Monday, the 1st of March, 1999. And if we can turn to the second page, please. And if we could -- actually, if we could move the page up a bit, because I need to look at the bottom of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see at the bottom of the page, sir, there's a paragraph which says the following: "A notorious Albanian collaborationist with the Serbian police, Muharem Ibraj -" that's you - "killed a local Albanian in Osek Hilja village near Gjakove, LDK sources said. The Albanian, Sulejman M. Bajrami, age 45, was killed after having had his house surrounded by Serbian forces." Now, this information was reported by the political party that you said that you belonged to. Can you explain why the party that you belonged to would describe you as "a notorious Albanian collaborationist with the Serbian police"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Why wasn't this report made at the beginning of the statement, when the killing was done? Second, the law existed. The state existed. There are documents. I don't have the document myself, but these documents exist. The court in Peja is in possession of documents and everything has been clarified. There were ten people. One of them was killed and nine others escaped. If it had been for the Serbian forces, everyone would have been killed, not just one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you say if it had been up to the Serbian forces everyone there would have been killed, not just one person? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Because here it says that the Serbian forces. Serbian forces were not there. Here it was only a group of ten people, Albanians belonging to the local defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the local defence force, the group of local defencemen that you led. You were there; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why your political party would refer to you in such disparaging terms as "a notorious Albanian collaborationist with the Serbian police"? That was my original question, but you haven't answered it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The Democratic Party gave this statement because I did not support them at the time. I have neither been against the Democratic Party -- I haven't been against the Democratic Party, and I haven't been against the state as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document, sir. If I can ask for the usher's patient assistance one more time. This is another printout from the Internet. It's a printout from the website of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina. It's their report number 461. It's entitled "On the Violation of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosova from 1 March Until 7 March, 1999." If we can turn to the second page, please. At the top of that page there's a paragraph that starts with the word "28 February." And that paragraph says the following: "The so-called local police, led by Muharem Ibraj from Osek Hilja, and the Serbian police, raided the house of and executed Sulejman Myftar Bajrami, age 45, in the presence of his family members. They arrested his guests, Xhavit Osmani and Bajram Luli." Now, again, why would this organisation say that you executed this man if you were merely acting in self-defence? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I have given a statement as regards this event. However, this organisation, not only for me but also for all those Albanians who did not cooperate with them, they wrote the same things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And none of these statements that you say exist that demonstrate that you acted in self-defence, none of those statements are with you here today. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe he said, Mr. Saxon, that the investigating judge gave him a verdict of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any documentation supporting what you said regarding the verdict of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No, I do not have with me -- such documents with me, because when I left Kosova I did not take anything with me. I fled Kosova, so I was unable to take any documents with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you managed to take the document that you presented to the Trial Chamber about an hour ago with you. You seemed to manage to take that document with you, D361, which allegedly is a threat against you from the KLA. Wouldn't it also have been important to take documents related to your legal situation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: The letter that the KLA sent me, I have kept it with me all along, and I even searched for the person who wrote the letter, and I wanted to ask him why they sent me the letter, whereas the verdict of self-defence didn't -- I wasn't interested in holding it with me all the time. The court documents are there, the documents must be there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity was the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document, sir. And we have an Albanian version of this document, so if that could also be given to the witness as well so he can read along. And if a copy could be placed on the ELMO, please. This document comes from another Kosovo website, known as Llapi. I also believe it's called in the Albanian language Forumi Shqiptar. And there is an entry posted on this website from April 2004 by a man named Faton Mehmetaj. And Mr. Usher, if you could turn the page to the second page, please, and Mr. Ibraj, if you could follow along with me on the second page of the Albanian version. From the middle of the second page of the English version and at the top of the second page in the Albanian version, the author asks the following question: "Why are some Albanian-speaking criminals, like Muharem Ibraj and others of his calibre who participated in many inconceivable crimes, rapes and tortures, free? They have criminal files and are known in the massacres of Beleg, Meja, Gjakove, Lubeniq, Bistrazin, etc." Is it still your position, sir, that you and the local defence force you led do not have a reputation for violence in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: If these statements were true, the local police would not have existed during the wartime, and someone would have killed us like they have killed police, soldiers, army generals, have bombed and all these things. The statements have been issued after the KFOR came there and people could do and say what they wanted, what they liked, because during the time that the state existed, whoever committed a crime, even a petty crime, he would end up in gaol and be sentenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you pointed out, sir, after the war ended in 1999, people could come back, people had been expelled, and as you put it, say what they wanted, what they liked; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because prior to that time, Kosovo Albanians who were disloyal to the Serb regime could not do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was a very simple question. If you can't answer it, I will simply move on. Do you recall what you were doing on the morning of 20th --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I am not understanding your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I will repeat it, then. After the war ended in 1999, when people who had been expelled came back, as you put it, they could say what they wanted, correct, because they couldn't do that under the Serb regime?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: After the war was over, I fled Kosova, and I don't know what happened in Kosova after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what you were doing on the 27th of April, 1999, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where your so-called local defence unit was operating on that morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what the local defence unit did that morning or which place it was. I know that it existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few days before the 27th of April, the police officer Milutin Prascevic and some others had been killed near Gjakove; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I heard that they were killed in the Meja village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I ask the usher's assistance again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at this photograph, sir, if you will. No, that's -- I apologise. That's the wrong photograph. Of the witness. Sir, this young woman's name is Merfidete Selmani. She's from the village of Dobroz in the municipality of Gjakove. Do you know anything about her?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything that might impinge upon her character or her ability to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't know this woman, and I don't recall to have ever seen her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put this -- this statement of this woman in front of you, sir, and on the ELMO, so that people can follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness, Merfidete Selmani, testified on the 16th of July, 2002. Her statement was entered into evidence under Rule 92 bis as Exhibit 265.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you see, this young woman travelled through Meja on that day, on the 27th of April, a few days after the policeman was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, if you could turn to page 5, please, of the statement. First of all, I need to read something at the bottom of page 5. Move the page up a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last paragraph begins: "Just before approaching Meja at about 1200 hours, I saw Serbian policemen who were outside the house located on top of a hill and at the foot of the hill close to a meadow. The convoy was proceeding slowly. We passed a vulcaniser (tyre repair shop) in Meja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, just a minute. We're checking to see whether that witness was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe that she was, Your Honour. I'm -- I'm virtually certain that she was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you using a redacted copy or an original?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time I'm using an unredacted copy, Your Honour, because it's my understanding that this was not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Bench was told that the exhibit was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't understand why that would be, and that is news to me, Your Honour. Can I -- perhaps simply to simplify matters, could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we're getting some information now. You can proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then proceeding to the top of page 6, the witness said the following: "There my father's uncle, Bajram Selmani, approximately 78 ... told us that Mush Jakupi was there with his sons. Bajram said that Muharem Jakupi had ordered Bajram's son, Jonuz Selmani, about 41 years old, to go out of the convoy and to run and join the place where the other men were detained. That is what I heard from Bajram Selmani in that moment. I knew that Mush Jakupi and his sons were Albanian local policemen from Osek Hilja, Djakovica/Gjakove, who were loyal to the Serbian regime. Actually, I knew that the Jakupis were very dangerous people; they were nasty famous among the Kosovo Albanian people. There was a common expression among the villagers that when someone was badly beaten, these would say that it was like if this person was beaten by Mush Jakupi gang. Muharem Jakupi was one of the sons of Mush." And then the witness continues to talk about how Bajram Selmani was beaten by Bajram Jakupi, son of Mush. Still your position the same, sir, that you and the local defence force that you led in 1999 did not have a reputation as violent criminals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Mush Jakupi is 83 years old. He's not capable of beating his own wife or someone else. Nobody dared meddle with the local defence or those who were working there. Whoever did something against the law, then the SUP was dealing with those cases and those persons were -- were responsible to the SUP. We -- none of us dared go to that area because it was a mountainous area and there were KLA members. Just an example: Mihil Abazi's brother was dead in Ramoc. He went to take part in the funeral --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you, sir. You tried to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said -- Mr. Saxon, when we talk here about local defence, is that the same as the local security position that the witness held? Is that your assumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the basis on which you are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That they are synonymous, Your Honour. Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I've heard the phrase "local defence," "local security," even "local police," used interchangeably, and you'll see them Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the statements that are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one dared meddle with the local defence because they knew if they did, the local -- the members of the local defence, including yourself, would respond quite brutally. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how Mush Jakupi could have given this statement when he is an invalid, or he is 83 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the statement of another witness, sir, who also places members of your unit at Meja, the day when hundreds of Kosovo Albanians were disappeared and killed. This is -- if this could be provided to the persons in the courtroom because it has not yet -- it has not been admitted into evidence, nor has it been provided to the Defence. And if we could turn, please, to page 5 of this statement. It's a woman by the name of Fatime Hoxha from the town of Gjakove. Actually, she lived in Junik until the war. And on the bottom of page 5, the last paragraph, she describes what she saw when she arrived at a checkpoint at Meja on the 27th of April, 1999. She said this: "I recognised among the perpetrators at the checkpoint in Meja the members of the Albanian family Jakupi who were members of the regular Serbian police. The Jakupis are from the village of Osek, Djakovica. I have known them for ten years. In Meja, I saw Mush Jakupi, approximately 50-55 years old, and his two sons whose names I do not know, and Muharem Jakupi, who is in his 40s. They were wearing the regular blue police uniforms with the insignia 'Milicija.' I begged them to release my relatives but they cursed me in Albanian and told me to go to Albania." That's on page 6. Sir, how is it that you just told us that members of your local security unit or local defence unit couldn't go to these areas and we now have two witnesses who said that they were there, they were at Meja, and they were involved in crimes against civilians on the 27th of April? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I think you very well know that they are false witnesses, because Mush Jakupi, I told even earlier, he is 83 years old and not 55 years old. I am 51 myself. And we never dared wear -- we couldn't even think of wearing police uniforms because we had our own uniforms. And we never had anything to do with the police. Meja is in another place. Osek is at another entrance. There is a distance between Meja and Osek. I may tell you that I wasn't in Meja until two, three years before the war, because it is situated in another area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Meja is just to the west of the town of Djakovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's approximately five to ten kilometres from the town where you lived, Osek Hilja; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware, sir, that more than 200 bodies of persons who disappeared at Meja on the 27th of April, 1999, have been exhumed in the town of Batajnica, close to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I have heard about that after I came to Nis. I saw it in a book on the kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you suppose those bodies got there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: I told you, it was in 2000 that I read about that for this event. In that book you can find the names of my -- of the six members of my own family as well. But before that, I had -- I had no knowledge of this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Can we look at the next document, please. It's the statement of Durim Domi. And if copies could be distributed to members of the courtroom, please. This is another ICTY witness statement. It is not in evidence. And if a copy could be placed on the ELMO, please. Statement by a man named Durim Domi from the town of -- or the city of Gjakove itself. And if we could turn to the first page of the text of the statement, which is page 2. And this person is describing what he saw on the 27th of March, 1999, sir, from his house in Djakovica. And the third paragraph, the third sentence, he says this: "On the 27th of March I was in my courtyard together with my family. The police together with members of Mush Jakupi arrived and they broke into the courtyard by forcing the gate. All of us fled up to Qabrat hill. From there we saw police and Mush Jakupi unit members while they were burning the houses of Afrim Domi and Fatmir Domi." The next paragraph, it says: "One could recognise the members of Mush Jakupi unit because they wore plain clothes and they spoke Albanian. They used to cooperate with police. Mush Jakupi members used to report to the police which houses had to be burnt." Do you have any idea how it is that this witness saw the members of your local security unit burning houses in Gjakove on the 27th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: This is not true. Neither myself nor any of the members of the local defences ever torched a house, a single house, or even the smallest object, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, finally, another statement, of Mr. Dervishdana. If we could turn to -- this is a statement not in evidence, given to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a statement given to the ICTY by a man named Myrvet Dervishdana, who lived on Ymer Grezda Street, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A woman, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A female.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned during your direct testimony, sir, that you knew Mr. Emin Dervishdana. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 8 of this statement, please. Because this statement describes the events on the 25th of March in Djakovica on Ymer Grezda Street, and if we could go to the top of the page, please. The second paragraph, the witness describes how her brother Emin, the man you knew, "... saw an Albanian man, a certain Mush Jakupi, and his group on Ymer Grezda Street. Mush Jakupi was a MUP officer. Before the massacre, I was told by my brother Emin that that day Mush Jakupi's unit was patrolling Ymer Grezda Street. On the same date three Albanian civilians were killed inside a house in the Tyrbe area..." Do you still maintain the same position, sir, that you and the members of your local security unit do not have a reputation for violence? Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ
utterances.text: With respect to Tyrbe, Dervishdana was a dervish, a Muslim priest, and even if he turned his gun to fire at me I would have never killed him because he was a religious person. As far as Mush Jakupi is concerned, he was a MUP officer. Being a Serb officer, then I'm happy to hear that Serbia was still keeping in its ranks officers of the age of 83 years and invalids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will just note that once again you have not answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the hour. It's a quarter to two. I can stop here and take just a few more minutes tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. I should say that the correct number for the exhibit admitted today is D302 not D361. The Registrar will have to find a way to compensate Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of August, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
